title: ADGRG1-targeted hypoxia preconditioned extracellular vesicles ameliorate intervertebral disc degeneration by delivering taurine to disrupt the oxidative stress feedback loop-driven ferroptosis in nucleus pulposus cells

sections.abstract: Cervical spondylosis and low back pain caused by intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) are among the leading causes of clinical disability. Although excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) are established drivers of IVDD, the mechanisms linking ROS accumulation to disc cell dysfunction, cell death programs, and disruption of intervertebral disc tissue homeostasis remain insufficiently elucidated, limiting the development of effective redox-targeted therapies. Here, we revealed the "ROS-Mitochondrial dysfunction-Ferritinophagy" oxidative stress feedback loop serves as the central mechanism driving ROS-induced nucleus pulposus cell (NPC) ferroptosis to promote IVDD progression. Furthermore, we identified the membrane protein ADGRG1 as a biomarker of ROS-induced ferroptosis in injured NPCs and developed ADGRG1-tethered peptide (A1TP)-modified hypoxia preconditioned extracellular vesicles (HX-EVs) with targeted antioxidant therapeutic potential. The engineered HX-EVs selectively accumulated in injured NPCs and delivered high levels of taurine, which bound to LKB1 (Glu165, Arg301) and MO25 (Arg194, Leu197) residues to facilitate the assembly of the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 kinase complex. This interaction regulated the expression of NCOA4 and TFAM by activating the AMPK/NRF2 signaling pathway, which suppressed ferritinophagy, enhanced mitochondrial repair and regeneration, and protected NPCs from ROS-induced ferroptosis, ultimately facilitating the repair of degenerated intervertebral discs. In summary, the A1TP-HX-EV system developed in this study provides a promising theranostic application for IVDD and offers valuable insights into the mechanisms of targeted HX-EV delivery and intervertebral disc regeneration.
sections.introduction:
Cervical spondylosis and low back pain caused by intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) are major chronic diseases that seriously endanger human health and are also one of the main causes of clinical disability [ 1 ]. In 2020, approximately 619 million people worldwide suffered from low back pain, and projections indicate this figure could reach 843 million by 2050, placing a substantial burden on patients' health and socioeconomic systems [ 2 , 3 ]. The pathogenesis of IVDD involves a complex signaling network and various effector molecules, including genetic susceptibility, oxidative stress, immune dysregulation, cell death, and mitochondrial dysfunction [ 4 , 5 ]. However, the precise molecular mechanisms that exacerbate IVDD progression and potential therapeutic targets remain unclear. Multiple studies have revealed that although the clinical etiology of IVDD is multifactorial, a major contributing factor is the elevated level of reactive oxygen species (ROS) within the intervertebral discs (IVD) [ 6 , 7 ]. During the process of IVDD, factors such as cellular senescence, mechanical stress, and inflammatory responses induce injury to nucleus pulposus cells (NPCs), rapidly triggering early alarm responses that cause mitochondrial impairment and excessive ROS production mediated by NADPH oxidases [ 8 ]. The imbalance between ROS generation and clearance disrupts redox homeostasis, resulting in oxidative damage to intracellular macromolecules and subsequent dysfunction of NPCs [ 9 ]. As the predominant cell type within the IVD, the loss of NPCs leads to extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation and reduced IVD hydration, resulting in decreased IVD height and functional impairment. Ultimately, this process causes compressive injury to spinal nerves and pain [ 8 , 10 ]. Therefore, elucidating the molecular mechanisms by which excessive ROS accumulation in injured NPCs drives disc cell dysfunction, cell death programs, and disruption of intervertebral disc tissue homeostasis, and developing targeted therapeutic strategies to mitigate ROS-mediated cellular senescence, apoptosis, or ferroptosis hold great significance for preventing IVDD and slowing the progression of degenerative disc disease.

Extracellular vesicles (EVs) mediate intercellular communication by transferring informational molecules such as nucleic acids, proteins, and bioactive small molecules, and are considered a promising cell-free therapy for IVDD [ 11 ]. Recent studies have revealed that hypoxia preconditioned mesenchymal stem cell derived extracellular vesicles (HX-EVs) play an important role in regulating anti-oxidative stress and inflammation [ 12 , 13 ]. Moreover, the unique advantages of EVs, including their drug-loading capacity and modifiable surface properties, enable the incorporation of targeting ligands, therapeutic agents, and imaging probes within a single vesicle while preserving functionality. These features make HX-EVs highly promising candidates as theranostic carriers for targeting ROS-injured NPCs [ 14 ]. However, the clinical application of EVs still faces challenges related to low delivery efficiency, including poor targeting specificity and rapid clearance by the immune system, which limit their bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. Surface modification and drug-loading strategies can help overcome these limitations by reducing off-target effects, shortening cellular internalization time, and enhancing therapeutic precision [ 15 ]. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop engineered HX-EVs equipped with customized targeting molecules, therapeutic agents, and imaging probes to formulate an integrated theranostic strategy. The inclusion of imaging agents enables accurate, visual, and informative monitoring, facilitating early NPC-targeted therapeutic interventions to promote IVD regeneration. To achieve this, we sought to identify reliable molecular recognition targets for injured NPCs in IVDD therapy.

Through in vitro experiments identifying key biomarkers associated with ROS-induced NPC injury, followed by validation in clinical degenerative nucleus pulposus (NP) tissues and IVDD animal model, we found that ADGRG1 (GPR56), an adhesion G protein-coupled receptor (aGPCR), is positively correlated with the severity of intervertebral disc degeneration and accurately reflects the extent of ROS-mediated NPC injury. In human hematopoietic stem cells, functional stem cells after in vitro expansion are enriched in a population with low mitochondrial ROS that expresses high levels of ADGRG1, suggesting ADGRG1 marks or supports cells that better tolerate oxidative stress [ 16 ]. ADGRG1 contributes to the regulation of cell adhesion, survival, and anti-apoptotic signaling pathways, which protect cells from oxidative stress and cell death [ 17 ]. Therefore, the rapid upregulation of ADGRG1 on the surface of injured NPCs may represent part of a protective response against ROS-induced injury. These pathophysiological findings suggest that developing ADGRG1-targeted therapeutic strategies to specifically recognize and treat ROS-injured NPCs may offer a promising approach for the treatment of IVDD.

Here, we describe the development of a therapeutic strategy using HX-EVs engineered for ADGRG1 targeting, incorporating both therapeutic and imaging functionalities, to selectively bind injured NPCs for evaluation and targeted treatment of IVDD. Initially, we verified the feasibility of ADGRG1 as a molecular target specifically binding to injured NPCs in a rat model of puncture-induced IVDD. Next, we modified the membrane of hypoxia-preconditioned human placental mesenchymal stem cell (pMSC)-derived EVs with an ADGRG1-tethered peptide (7-mer peptide, TYFAVLM, A1TP). By conjugating A1TP to a polyethylene glycol-linked phospholipid derivative (DSPE-PEG) without introducing additional amino acids, we generated engineered antioxidant MSC-EVs with ADGRG1-targeting capability (A1TP-HX-EVs). After confirming the targeting ability of A1TP-HX-EVs using molecular imaging, we investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying the disc-protective effects of high levels of taurine (2-aminoethanesulfonic acid) loaded in HX-EVs using high-precision liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and molecular docking techniques. Overall, our study establishes an HX-EV-based therapeutic strategy that specifically targets degenerative NPCs in the intervertebral discs via ADGRG1, enabling both monitoring and treatment of IVDD.
sections.methods:
Male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats (8-10 weeks old) used in this study were purchased from Jinan Pengyue Experimental Animal Breeding Co., Ltd. (Shandong, China). All experimental protocols involving animals complied with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (Approval No.: 20190022). The intervertebral disc degeneration model was established as previously described [ 18 ]. Briefly, rats were anesthetized through an intraperitoneal administration of pentobarbital sodium (30 mg/kg; P3761, Sigma-Aldrich, GER) and positioned in the prone position. Disc levels were identified by palpation and confirmed by X-ray imaging. To induce varying degrees of IVDD (mild, moderate, severe), twelve healthy rats were randomly assigned in each experimental batch into four groups (n = 3 per group). The Co6/7 disc was punctured using 25G, 21G, or 18G needles, respectively, while unpunctured discs were retained as intact controls. For punctured discs, the needle tip was carefully inserted through the annulus fibrosus into the center of the nucleus pulposus to a controlled depth of 5 mm, rotated 360° twice, and held in place for 30 s before removal. All needles were pre-marked to ensure the depth did not exceed 5 mm. For the engineered extracellular vesicle treatment studies, twenty-five healthy rats were randomly assigned in each experimental batch into five groups (n = 5 per group), and the Co6/7 and Co8/9 tail discs were selected. Two weeks after puncture-induced disc injury using a 21G needle, when IVDD was established, 10 μg of EVs, HX-EVs, or A1TP-HX-EVs (5 μL) were injected into the degenerated disc using a 30G syringe. Following the procedure, rats were returned to standard housing and monitored for 8 weeks, during which no signs of pain or distress were observed.

Human placental mesenchymal stem cells (pMSCs) were isolated from placental tissue, which was digested with type II collagenase and trypsin, as previously described [ 19 ]. The isolated cells were cultured in DMEM/F-12 medium (C11330500BT, Gibco, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (10099141C, Gibco), 1 X MEM Non-Essential Amino Acids Solution (11140050, Gibco), 100 U/mL penicillin and 100 μg/mL streptomycin (A5873601, Gibco). For this study, pMSCs between passages 4 and 10 were used. Primary NPCs were isolated from nucleus pulposus tissues surgically removed from patients with mild IVDD (Pfirrmann grade 2). The tissues were digested with 0.2% type II collagenase for 5 h. The isolated NPCs were cultured in Nucleus pulposus cell medium (4801, ScienCell, USA). All cells were cultured at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 in a humidified incubator (Thermo Fisher, USA). For hypoxic treatment, cells were maintained in a humidified incubator at 37 °C under 5% CO 2 , 1% O 2 , and 94% N 2 . To mimic the oxidative microenvironment of intervertebral discs with varying degrees of degeneration, primary human NPCs were treated with 50 μM, 100 μM, or 200 μM tert-butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP) and incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 for 12 h (h). Subsequently, 100 μg/mL of EVs were added according to the experimental protocol and incubated for an additional 24 h.

The pMSCs were subcultured every two days in their respective media supplemented. During subculture, the culture supernatant was collected and sequentially centrifuged at 500× g for 10 min, 2000× g for 30 min, and 10,000× g for 30 min to remove cell debris and apoptotic bodies. The resulting supernatant was then ultracentrifuged at 100,000× g for 70 min to pellet EVs, followed by an additional ultracentrifugation at 100,000× g for 2 h in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to further purify them. The final EV pellet was resuspended in 200 μL PBS and stored at −80 °C. All procedures were performed under sterile conditions at 4 °C. The total protein content of EVs was quantified using a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) protein assay kit (23225, Thermo Fisher).

The MST assay was performed according to previously reported protocol [ 20 ]. Briefly, ADGRG1-GFP fusion protein and GFP control were expressed in 293T cells and subsequently purified according to standard procedures. The purified proteins (final concentration, 100 nM) were mixed with serially diluted A1TP ligand solutions (16 gradient concentrations ranging from 62.5 μM to 1.9 nM) prepared in assay buffer containing PBS supplemented with 0.05% Tween-20. Each 10 μL protein-ligand mixture was loaded into premium-coated glass capillaries and analyzed using a Monolith NT.115 instrument (NanoTemper Technologies, Germany). Measurements were acquired at 40% MST and 60% excitation power. Fluorescence intensity changes were recorded, and dissociation constants (KD) were calculated with the NanoTemper analysis software.

As shown in Fig. S6 , the peptide A1TP (TYFAVLM) was conjugated with Azido-PEG2-amine through an amidation reaction to obtain Azido-PEG2-A1TP. Specifically, 30 mg of the peptide was dissolved in 5 mL of DMSO buffer, and a mixture of EDC (10 mg, 22980, Thermo Fisher) and sulfo-NHS (20 mg, 24510, Thermo Fisher) was added to 500 μL of MES buffer (pH = 5.0) and stirred until fully dissolved. The prepared solution was added to the reaction mixture and incubated at room temperature for 30 min. Subsequently, Azido-PEG2-amine (18 mg; molar ratio peptide: Azido-PEG2-amine = 1: 3) was introduced, and the pH was adjusted to 7.0 with sodium bicarbonate. The mixture was stirred for 30 min at room temperature and then allowed to react overnight at 4 °C. After dilution, the reaction mixture was dialyzed against sterile water using a 100-500 Da cellulose dialysis membrane at 4 °C for 72 h to remove EDC, sulfo-NHS, and unreacted Azido-PEG2-amine. The resulting product was lyophilized to obtain Azido-PEG2-A1TP. Subsequently, Azido-PEG2-A1TP was conjugated with DSPE-PEG-Alkyne (MW 3400, HY-167028B, MedChemExpress) via click chemistry reaction. Under a nitrogen atmosphere, DSPE-PEG-Alkyne and Azido-PEG2-A1TP were dissolved in 5 mL of DMSO at a molar ratio of 1:1.5 (60 mg DSPE-PEG-Alkyne and 30 mg Azido-PEG2-A1TP). The reaction substrates, CuSO 4 , and sodium ascorbate were added at a molar ratio of 1:0.2:0.4, and the mixture was stirred at 37 °C under N 2 for 24 h. The resulting reaction mixture was diluted and transferred into a dialysis membrane (molecular weight cutoff: 2 kDa), followed by dialysis against sterile deionized water at 4 °C for 3 days to remove unreacted Azido-PEG2-A1TP, CuSO 4 , sodium ascorbate, and DMSO. The purified product was then lyophilized to obtain DSPE-PEG-A1TP powder, which was stored at −20 °C for further use. The characteristic proton nuclear magnetic resonance (^1H NMR) spectra were recorded using a Bruker AVANCE NEO 400 MHz NMR spectrometer, with deuterated DMSO (DMSO-d6) as the solvent. The FT-IR transmittance spectrum between 4000 and 400 cm −1 was recorded using a TENSOR II FT-IR spectrometer (Bruker, Germany).

DSPE-PEG-A1TP was dissolved in DMSO to a final storage concentration of 500 μM. To optimize the preparation conditions of A1TP-HX-EVs, DSPE-PEG-A1TP at different final molar concentrations (5, 10, and 15 μM) was incubated with EVs at 4 °C for 30 min. Excess DSPE-PEG-A1TP was then removed by ultrafiltration using 100 kDa centrifugal filters with fivefold volumes of PBS, repeated more than five times until the A1TP-HX-EVs were concentrated to their original volume. The optimal labeling concentration of DSPE-PEG-A1TP was determined to be 10 μM based on aggregation-induced emission (AIE) fluorescence visualization of the modified EVs. The particle size distribution and zeta potential of EVs, HX-EVs and A1TP-HX-EVs were measured using a Zetaview nanoparticle analyzer (Particle Metrix). The morphology of EVs, HX-EVs, and A1TP-HX-EVs was then examined by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (FEI Talos L120C, Thermo Fisher), as previously described. Briefly, EV samples (2 μg/μL) were placed on carbon-coated copper grids (Xinxing Bairui Technology Co., Ltd., China) and negatively stained with 2% uranyl acetate. After air drying, the samples were observed under TEM at an accelerating voltage of 120 kV. Finally, the presence of the characteristic EV markers Alix (92880, Cell Signaling Technology), CD81 (56039, Cell Signaling Technology) and TSG101 (sc-7964, Santa Cruz Biotechnology) was confirmed by Western blot analysis.

AIE fluorescence enables bright and stable emission upon EV internal aggregation, significantly enhancing visualization sensitivity [ 21 ]. To evaluate the targeting capability of A1TP-HX-EVs, both HX-EVs and A1TP-HX-EVs were incubated with 5 μM TTVP, an amphiphilic AIE fluorescent dye, at room temperature for 10 min. The samples were then transferred to 100 kDa MWCO ultrafiltration tubes (UFC510008, Merck), centrifuged, and washed to remove free dye. The AIE-labeled EVs were subsequently incubated with DSPE-PEG-A1TP at room temperature for 30 min, followed by ultrafiltration and washing to eliminate unbound DSPE-PEG-A1TP, yielding AIE-labeled A1TP-HX-EVs. For in vitro assays, NPCs either overexpressing ADGRG1 or subjected to TBHP (50, 100, or 200 μM) were treated with 100 μg/mL of AIE-labeled HX-EVs or A1TP-HX-EVs according to the experimental design. The cellular uptake and targeting efficiency within 24 h were visualized using a ZEISS live-cell imaging workstation (Celldiscoverer 7, GER). For in vivo experiments, mild and severe IVDD models were established. AIE-labeled A1TP-HX-EVs (10 μg in 5 μL) were injected intradiscally and allowed to act for 24 h. In a separate experiment, a moderate IVDD model was induced by 21G needle puncture, followed by intradiscal injection of AIE-labeled EVs, HX-EVs, or A1TP-HX-EVs (10 μg in 5 μL) for 24 h. After treatment, the IVDs were harvested, fixed, and cryosectioned into 5 μm slices for immunostaining of ADGRG1. Based on the AIE fluorescence properties of TTVP, confocal microscopy imaging was performed using excitation/emission wavelengths of 488/600 nm to assess the targeting and internalization of A1TP-HX-EVs.

Gaussia luciferase (Gluc)-labeled EVs were prepared as previously described [ 22 ]. Briefly, pMSCs were infected with lentiviral particles expressing a fusion protein of Gluc and human mucin (MOI = 10), followed by selection using 1 μg/mL puromycin (P4512, Sigma-Aldrich). Gluc-labeled EVs were subsequently harvested from the supernatant of Gluc-pMSCs via ultracentrifugation. Then, Gluc-labeled HX-EVs were incubated with DSPE-PEG-A1TP to obtain Gluc-labeled A1TP-HX-EVs (A1TP-Gluc-EVs). The mixture was centrifuged at 14,000× g for 10 min using 100 kDa MWCO ultrafiltration tubes (UFC510008, Merck) and washed with PBS to remove unbound DSPE-PEG-A1TP. Bioluminescence imaging of Gluc activity in EVs or A1TP-Gluc-EVs was performed using the IVIS Spectrum imaging system. For in vitro analysis, A1TP-Gluc-EVs were plated in 6-well plates, and bioluminescence was detected using 0.1 μg/mL coelenterazine (3031, Nanolight Technology, Pinetop, AZ) as the substrate. For in vivo imaging, Gluc-labeled A1TP-HX-EVs were injected into degenerated IVDs. At designated time points (0, 12, 24, 48, and 72 h), rats were immediately subjected to bioluminescence imaging following intraperitoneal injection of water-soluble coelenterazine (5 mg/kg). Bioluminescent signals were captured using the IVIS Spectrum system, and the radiance efficiency of regions of interest (ROIs) was quantified to assess the retention of A1TP-HX-EVs.

To evaluate the structural restoration of degenerated intervertebral discs, MRI and X-ray imaging were performed after two weeks of needle puncture-induced degeneration and eight weeks of treatment with engineered EVs. Sagittal T2-weighted MRI images of rat caudal intervertebral discs were acquired using a Siemens Verio magnetic resonance imaging system, and the degree of IVDD was assessed in a double-blinded manner according to the Pfirrmann grading system. In addition, sagittal X-ray images of rat caudal vertebrae were obtained using a Mobile Radiography System (Siemens Healthineers), and the disc height index (DHI) was calculated in a double-blinded fashion to quantitatively evaluate the recovery of disc height.

At designated time points, rats were euthanized, and tissue samples were collected for histological examination. After fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde and four weeks of decalcification in 0.5 M EDTA (pH = 7.2), samples were dehydrated using a graded ethanol series, cleared with xylene, and embedded in paraffin. Subsequently, 5 μm sections were prepared. For frozen sections, NP tissues were embedded directly in Optimal Cutting Temperature (OCT) compound without prior paraformaldehyde fixation, stored at −80 °C, and sectioned at −20 °C to a thickness of 5 μm. Paraffin sections were stained following standard protocols using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), Alcian Blue, Masson's trichrome, and Safranin O/Fast Green staining to evaluate IVD morphology and extracellular matrix composition. For tissue and cell immunofluorescence staining, paraffin-embedded sections were deparaffinized and subjected to antigen retrieval using sodium citrate buffer, followed by three washes with PBS. After permeabilization and blocking with 10% goat serum containing 0.2% Triton X-100, the sections were incubated with primary antibodies against ADGRG1 (1:50; sc-390192, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), TOM20(11802-1-AP, Proteintech), 4-HNE(68538-1-Ig, Proteintech), 4-HNE(HY-P81208, MCE), Ferritin (Rockland 200-401-090-0100), LAMP1(65051-1-Ig, Proteintech), PAX1(sc-514352, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), FOXF1(PA5-83039, Thermo Fisher). Cells cultured on glass coverslips were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and washed three times with PBS. After blocking with 10% goat serum, the samples were incubated with primary antibodies. After washing, sections were incubated with Alexa Fluor 488- or Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated secondary antibodies (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA), and nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (2.5 μg/mL). Confocal images were obtained with a ZEISS LSM800 laser scanning microscope, and quantitative analysis was performed using ImageJ software.

Nucleus pulposus tissues or cell pellets treated with EVs were fixed in a solution containing 2.5% glutaraldehyde and 2% paraformaldehyde, followed by postfixation in 1% osmium tetroxide. Samples were then dehydrated through a graded ethanol and acetone series, embedded in epoxy resin (SPI-Pon 812), and polymerized at 60 °C for 48 h. Ultrathin sections (70 nm) were mounted on 200-mesh copper grids and double-stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate. The mitochondrial ultrastructure was subsequently examined using a transmission electron microscope (FEI Talos L120C, Thermo Fisher).

The oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was assessed by using the Seahorse XF Cell Mito Stress Test Kit (103015-100, Agilent) according to the instructions with a Seahorse XFe24 extracellular flux analyzer (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Briefly, 2 × 10 4 NPCs were seeded into 24-well XF cell culture microplates (102342-100, Agilent) and subjected to TBHP-induced oxidative injury for 12 h, followed by treatment with engineered EVs for 24 h. On the day of measurement, the culture medium was replaced with XF DMEM base medium (103680-100, Agilent). Basal respiration was recorded, followed by sequential injections of 1.5 μM oligomycin, 2 μM carbonyl cyanide-4-(trifluoromethoxy) phenylhydrazone (FCCP), and 0.5 μM rotenone/antimycin A. The OCR values were normalized to the number of cells seeded per well. Maximal respiration was calculated as the difference between the maximum OCR after FCCP injection and the non-mitochondrial respiration OCR measured following rotenone and antimycin A treatment.

EVs and HX-EVs were lysed in 1 mL of ice-cold extraction solvent (methanol: acetonitrile: water = 2: 2: 1, v/v). The samples were subjected to homogenized at 35 Hz for 4 min, followed by sonication for 5 min, with the extraction process repeated three times. The lysates were vortexed and centrifuged at 16,000× g for 10 min at 4 °C to remove debris. The supernatant (10 μL) was injected into an Acquity Ultra Performance LC system for separation using a Waters Acquity Uplc Beh Amide column (2.1 mm × 50 mm, 1.7 μm). The mobile phase consisted of solvent A (H 2 O containing 25 mM ammonium acetate and 25 mM ammonia) and solvent B (acetonitrile). Mass spectrometry was performed on an Orbitrap Exploris 120 instrument operated in negative ion mode, and MS/MS data were subsequently analyzed.

SPR experiments were performed using a Biacore 8K system (Cytiva, Marlborough, MA, USA). Recombinant LKB1, MO25 (WT), and mutant proteins LKB1 (E165A, R301A) and MO25 (R194A, L197A) were immobilized on a Series S Sensor Chip CM5 (Cytiva) via amine coupling using a standard coupling kit (Cytiva) at pH 7.4. Binding analyses were conducted at 25 °C with a flow rate of 30 μL/min in PBS buffer (pH 7.4) containing 0.05% Tween 20 and 5% DMSO. Taurine was injected using an association phase of 120 s followed by a dissociation phase of 120 s. A twofold serial dilution of taurine was prepared, covering concentrations from 100 to 0.78 μM. DMSO solvent correction curves were generated by injecting a series of DMSO solutions ranging from 4.5% to 5.8% (v/v) in the running buffer. All sensorgrams were double-referenced by subtracting signals from both the reference flow cell and blank injections. Data were analyzed and fitted to a 1:1 Langmuir binding model using Biacore Insight Evaluation Software.

CRISPR/Cas9 technology was used to introduce point mutations at the LKB1 (E165A and R301A) and MO25 (R194A and L197A) sites. As previously described [ 23 ], briefly, three distinct guide RNAs (gRNAs) targeting the Glu165 and Arg301 loci of LKB1 were designed using the Integrated DNA Technologies design tool ( https://sg.idtdna.com/pages ) and individually cloned into the pX459 vector. Single-stranded donor oligonucleotides (ssODNs) containing 250 bp homology arms flanking the E165A and R301A mutation sites were synthesized. The pX459 plasmids and ssODNs were co-transfected into Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-immortalized nucleus pulposus cells. Following transfection, genomic PCR sequencing was performed to screen for LKB1 E165A and R301A mutant clones. The validated LKB1 mutant nucleus pulposus cell clones were subsequently used to generate MO25 (R194A and L197A) point mutations following the same procedure. The sequence information for the gRNAs used for gene editing and the shRNAs employed for gene knockdown has been provided in the Supplementary Table.

For immunoblotting, cells were lysed on ice using RIPA lysis buffer (P0013, Beyotime Biotechnology). NP tissues were isolated from rat IVDs and homogenized on ice in RIPA buffer supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (P8340-1 ML, Sigma-Aldrich) using a tissue homogenizer for 30 min and total protein concentrations were determined with BCA protein assay kit (23225, Thermo Fisher). The supernatant was collected, mixed with 5 × SDS-PAGE loading buffer, and boiled at 95 °C for 5 min. Equal amounts of protein were separated by 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes (Millipore, Germany). Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk for 2 h, incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, and then incubated with secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature. Primary antibodies included FTH1(4393S, Cell Signaling Technology), COL1A1(72026T, Cell Signaling Technology), COL2A1(sc-52658, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), MMP13(ab39012, Abcam), GPX4(30388-1-AP, Proteintech), ADGRG1(sc-390192, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), TAUT (sc-393036, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), TonEBP (sc-101098, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), CDO1 (12589-1-AP, Proteintech), AMPK(10929-2-AP, Proteintech), Phospho-AMPK (Thr172)(2535T, Cell Signaling Technology), SIRT1(8469T, Cell Signaling Technology), P-SIRT1(Ser47)(2314S, Cell Signaling Technology), PGC-1α(2178S, Cell Signaling Technology), Ac-lysine(sc-81623, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), NRF2(16396-1-AP, Proteintech), TFAM(22586-1-AP, Proteintech), NCOA4(66849S, Santa Cruz Biotechnology).

For immunoprecipitation (IP), cells were lysed in IP lysis buffer containing 150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris, 1% NP-40, 10 mM NaF, 20 mM β-glycerophosphate, 1 mM EDTA (pH = 8.0), and 2 mM Na 3 VO 4 (pH = 7.5), supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (P8340-1 ML, Sigma-Aldrich). The cell lysates were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. The primary antibodies included LKB1 (sc-32245, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), MO25 (2716S, Cell Signaling Technology), and STRAD (sc-515635, Santa Cruz Biotechnology). The following day, pre-washed Pierce™ Protein A/G magnetic beads (88802, Thermo Fisher) were added and incubated for 2 h at room temperature. The beads were then washed three times with IP lysis buffer, and the immunoprecipitates were analyzed by immunoblotting or LC-MS/MS.

All experiments were independently repeated at least three times under each condition to ensure reproducibility. Data are presented as scatter plots showing the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical analysis between two groups was conducted using a two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, whereas multiple group comparisons were evaluated by one-way or two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test to assess intergroup differences. Statistical analyses were performed by using GraphPad Prism software, with P-values ( P ) < 0.05 considered statistically significant.
sections.results:
Nucleus pulposus cell attenuation is a crucial cause of intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). To explore the key molecular mechanisms of IVDD, we compared single-cell RNA sequencing data of surgically removed NP tissue samples from patients with Mild (MI) and Severe (SE) IVDD. Based on characteristic marker genes, we defined 10 cell populations, including NPCs, Chondrocytes, Fibroblasts, Macrophages, and endothelial cells ( Fig. 1 A–B). Subsequently, all NPCs were selected using PAX1 and FOXF1, two NPC markers ( Fig. 1 C). The enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between the two groups of NPCs revealed that the ferroptosis pathway was activated in NPCs with severe IVDD ( Fig. 1 D and S1A ). In addition, GSEA enrichment analysis also showed that IVDD, ferroptosis, and oxidative stress damage-related genes were mainly expressed in severely degenerated NP tissues ( Fig. 1 E and S1B ). The above results indicated that NPCs with severe IVDD have serious levels of ROS oxidative stress damage and ferroptosis. To further confirm the results of single-cell sequencing analysis, we extracted samples of degenerated nucleus pulposus from clinical IVDD patients and found that the expression level of matrix metalloproteinase 13 (MMP13) increased, and the normal nucleus pulposus extracellular matrix structural protein COL2 was degraded, showing more severe IVDD characteristics. More importantly, we found that Nuclear Receptor Coactivator 4 (NCOA4), a key mediator of ferritinophagy that transports ferritin (FTH) to lysosomes for degradation [ 24 ], was highly expressed in severely degenerated NP tissues and promoted FTH degradation, while the expression of Glutathione Peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a key inhibitory molecule that protects cells from ferroptosis, was significantly suppressed ( Fig. 1 F–G). In addition, ROS levels and labile ferrous ion (Fe 2+ ) levels were significantly upregulated in severely degenerated NP tissues, and the death level of NPCs increased in severe IVDD, further confirming that NPCs with severe IVDD have severe ferroptosis ( Fig. 1 H–I and S1C). It is well known that mitochondria are key cells for the production and elimination of ROS in cells, and their health is another important factor in the initiation of ferroptosis [ 25 ]. In view of this, we conducted GSEA enrichment analysis and found that NPCs with severe IVDD had mitochondrial dysfunction and that genes related to mitochondrial impairment and membrane permeabilization were highly expressed ( Fig. 1 J and S1D ). Immunofluorescence analysis showed that the level of lipid peroxidation (LP) product 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE) in severely degenerated NP tissues was higher, and the number of mitochondria was lower ( Fig. 1 K–M), In addition, transmission electron microscopy imaging showed that mitochondrial cristae of NPCs with severe IVDD were missing and the mitochondrial membrane edges were blurred, reflecting severe mitochondrial damage ( Fig. 1 L and M). In summary, our results indicated that ROS-induced severe ferroptosis in NPCs, accompanied by severe damage to mitochondrial structure and function, is the major cause of aggravated IVDD. Therefore, inhibiting the release of ferrous ions and promoting the recovery of mitochondrial structure and number are the keys to effectively reduce ROS and promote the repair of degenerative discs. In order to precisely deliver therapeutics to NPCs induced by ROS damage and ferroptosis, we first screened feasible molecular targets that specifically bind to NPCs with ferroptosis. We identified extracted human primary NPCs by staining with characteristic markers PAX1 and FOXF1 ( Fig. S1E–F ). To simulate ROS damage in vivo and induce ferroptosis in NPCs in vitro , we used different concentrations of tert-Butyl hydroperoxide solution (TBHP) to induce ROS damage in NPCs for 12 h. We found that increasing concentrations of TBHP progressively elevated intracellular ROS levels, ferritinophagy, labile ferrous iron accumulation, and cell death rates in NPCs ( Fig. 2 A and S2A–C ), and concomitantly activated ferroptosis signaling pathways ( Fig. S2D ). In vitro treatment of ROS-injured NPCs with the selective ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin-1, a lipophilic chain-breaking radical-trapping antioxidant [ 26 ], effectively reduced ferritinophagy and ROS levels, thereby suppressing NPC ferroptosis ( Fig. S2E–G ). Collectively, these results indicated that ferroptosis is a principal mechanism underlying ROS-induced NPC death. Furthermore, RNA transcriptomic sequencing analysis (RNA-seq) and western blotting revealed that TBHP promotes the expression of genes associated with ROS-induced injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, and ferroptosis in NPCs ( Fig. 2 B–C), while suppressing the expression of genes related to mitochondrial function and regeneration ( Fig. S2H ). To further elucidate the interplay among ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction, and ferroptosis, NPCs were treated with the ferroptosis inducer Erastin, which triggers ferritinophagy [ 27 ]. Erastin treatment led to mitochondrial damage, elevated ROS levels ( Fig. S3A–D ). Similarly, treatment with the mitochondrial toxin Rotenone, an inhibitor of respiratory chain complex I that impairs mitochondrial function, resulted in increased ROS production and enhanced ferritinophagy in NPCs ( Fig. S3E–I ). Collectively, these findings demonstrated that ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction, and ferritinophagy form a mutually reinforcing positive feedback loop that drives oxidative stress and accelerates NPC death. Notably, by integrative analysis of differentially expressed genes identified by RNA-seq in TBHP-induced NPC injury and differentially expressed proteins identified by proteomic profiling in ROS-induced injury, we found that the expression of a type of G protein-coupled receptor protein ADGRG1 on the NPC cell membrane was significantly upregulated after TBHP induction ( Fig. 2 D and S4A-C ). More importantly, the expression of ADGRG1 gradually increased in parallel with the severity of TBHP-induced ferritinophagy and ferroptosis in NPCs ( Fig. 2 C). Immunofluorescence analysis further revealed a strong positive correlation between ADGRG1 expression and the ferroptosis marker 4-HNE ( Fig. 2 E–F). To validate this finding in vivo , we further confirmed that in a rat model of puncture-induced IVDD, ADGRG1 expression increased significantly and progressively with the severity of IVDD ( Fig. 2 G–H and S4D). Analysis of clinical samples revealed that higher ADGRG1 protein levels were associated with more severe IVDD ( Fig. 2 I, J and L), and showed a positive correlation with the ferroptosis marker 4-HNE ( Fig. 2 K–L). However, knockdown of ADGRG1 in NPCs did not directly disrupt the "ROS–mitochondrial dysfunction–ferritinophagy" positive feedback loop–mediated cellular injury ( Fig. S4E–L ). Although ADGRG1 silencing slightly increased TBHP-induced ROS accumulation and intracellular labile ferrous iron levels, these changes were not statistically significant. Consequently, depletion of ADGRG1 did not markedly increase the susceptibility of NPCs to ROS-induced ferroptosis ( Fig. S4E–L ). Collectively, these findings confirmed that the oxidative stress damage driven by "ROS-mitochondrial dysfunction-ferritinophagy" feedback loop represents a crucial pathological mechanism accelerating NPC death. ADGRG1 serves as an important membrane biomarker of oxidative stress feedback loop-driven ferroptosis in NPCs and may act as both a molecular indicator for assessing IVDD severity and a critical target for targeted delivery of therapeutic agents.

To construct a delivery and repair molecular system that could target injured NPCs and achieve delivery of hypoxia-preconditioned stem cell derived extracellular vesicles (HX-EVs) for repairing ROS-induced ferroptosis damage in NPCs, we designed engineered HX-EVs specifically targeting ADGRG1. Previous studies have revealed that ADGRG1 undergoes autoproteolysis at a conserved site between its extracellular domain and seven-transmembrane (7TM) domain, generating an N-terminal ADGRG1-tethered peptide (TYFAVLM, A1TP) that participates in the functional regulation of ADGRG1 [ 28 , 29 ]. Protein sequence alignment analysis showed that this A1TP is highly conserved across species ( Fig. S5A ). Induced-fit docking analysis indicated that A1TP possesses strong target-recognition capability ( Fig. 3 A and S5B ), More importantly, we directly confirmed the specific binding of A1TP to ADGRG1 protein using microscale thermophoresis, with a dissociation constant (KD) of 3.53 ± 0.29 μM ( Fig. 3 B). To conjugate A1TP to phospholipid-like molecules for engineering EV labeling, A1TP was linked to a PEG-based crosslinker to form the A1TP-PEG structure. Induced-fit docking and molecular dynamics simulations showed that A1TP-PEG exhibits a binding mode, stable binding free energy, and post-binding structural stability comparable to unconjugated PEG ( Fig. 3 C–D and S5C-F ), indicating that PEG as a crosslinker does not compromise A1TP's recognition of ADGRG1. Subsequently, we modified the ADGRG1-tethered peptide (A1TP) on the surface of EVs by using a hydrophobic insertion strategy to fabricate A1TP‐engineered hypoxia-induced pMSC EVs (A1TP-HP‐EVs) with the ability to identify and bind ADGRG1 on injured NPCs ( Fig. 3 E). DSPE (1,2-Distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphorylethanolamine) is a phospholipid-like structure used in various applications, particularly in drug delivery systems. We conjugated A1TP to 6-azidohexanoic acid via an amide reaction to generate Azido-PEG2-A1TP, and then further linked Azido-PEG2-A1TP to DSPE-PEG-Alkyne via click chemistry to form DSPE-PEG-A1TP, which could be inserted into EV membrane ( Fig. 3 E and S6 ). The newly generated triazole ring in the click chemistry reaction exhibited a characteristic C=N stretching vibration with a peak at ∼1538 cm −1 , indicating that A1TP binds to DSPE via chemical click reaction ( Fig. 3 F and S7A-B ). The hydrogen signatures of the phenyl and phenol groups at 7.5-8.0 ppm confirmed the successful synthesis of DSPE-PEG-ADGRG1 ( Fig. 3 G and S7C-D ). To investigate the targeted reparative effects of A1TP-HX-EVs, primary NPCs were treated in vitro with TBHP to induce injury, followed by incubation with A1TP-HX-EVs. Compared with EVs, HX-EVs more effectively reduced TBHP-induced ROS accumulation, and A1TP-HX-EVs further enhanced this antioxidant effect. Dose–response analysis of A1TP-HX-EVs revealed that a minimum concentration of 100 μg/mL was sufficient to significantly reduce intracellular ROS levels while maintaining robust antioxidant efficacy ( Fig. S9B–C ). Importantly, A1TP-HX-EVs significantly decreased intracellular levels of ferrous ions, thereby attenuating ferroptosis in NPCs ( Fig. 4 F and S9D ). RNA-seq revealed that A1TP-HX-EVs effectively downregulated gene sets associated with ROS-induced ferroptosis and oxidative damage in NPCs ( Fig. 4 G). Mechanistically, A1TP-HX-EVs suppressed ferritin degradation, thereby reducing ferrous ion release and iron overload, while promoting GPX4 expression to facilitate lipid peroxide breakdown and attenuate ferroptosis in NPCs ( Fig. 4 H). In addition, A1TP-HX-EVs decreased the expression of ADGRG1 and IVD degenerative marker MMP13, and enhanced the recovery of COL2 levels, contributing to extracellular matrix reconstruction ( Fig. 4 H and S9E ). Notably, we found that A1TP-HX-EVs more effectively enhanced the expression of genes related to the mitochondrial respiratory chain and mitochondrial biogenesis while suppressing abnormal respiratory chain activity ( Fig. 4 I and S9F ). Mitochondrial stress assays further confirmed that A1TP-HX-EVs improved mitochondrial function by increasing maximal respiration ( Fig. 4 J–K), thereby reducing ROS levels through efficient respiratory chain operation. Immunofluorescence analysis further demonstrated that A1TP-HX-EVs promoted mitochondrial regeneration and decreased lipid peroxide accumulation, ultimately inhibiting ferroptosis in NPCs ( Fig. 4 L and S9G ). Taken together, these results demonstrated that A1TP-HX-EVs could effectively target and recognize ROS-injured NPCs, promote their cellular internalization, inhibit ferritin degradation, and restore mitochondrial function. These effects collectively reduce intracellular ROS levels and lipid peroxidation, which suppressed oxidative stress feedback loop-driven ferroptosis in NPCs.

To investigate the in vivo targeting and internalization of A1TP-HX-EVs, we established intervertebral discs (IVD) with varying degrees of degeneration. Since the IVD is an avascular tissue and systemic administration of EVs often results in rapid clearance or accumulation in organs such as the liver, spleen, and lungs, effective delivery via vascular injection is limited [ 30 ]. Therefore, we administered A1TP-HX-EVs through direct intradiscal injection. Immunofluorescence analysis showed that ADGRG1 expression increased in NPCs with severe IVDD, promoting greater internalization of AIE-labeled A1TP-HX-EVs into degenerative NPCs. Importantly, fluorescence colocalization demonstrated that A1TP-HX-EVs predominantly entered NPCs with high ADGRG1 expression ( Fig. 5 A). To further investigate the in vivo reparative effects of A1TP-HX-EVs on degenerative IVD, we established rat tail IVDD models via needle puncture and administered intradiscal injection of A1TP-HX-EVs once weekly for three weeks ( Fig. S10E ). Eight weeks after treatment, MRI scans showed that A1TP-HX-EVs more effectively reduced the grade of IVDD ( Fig. 5 E and F). Additionally, treatment significantly increased the disc height index (DHI) and mitigated degenerative IVD collapse ( Fig. 5 F and G). Histopathological analysis revealed that, compared with EVs, HX-EVs more effectively promoted nucleus pulposus regeneration following IVDD. Notably, engineered A1TP-HX-EVs exhibited the greatest therapeutic effect, characterized by significant restoration of glycosaminoglycans and glycoproteins in the extracellular matrix, along with effective suppression of NP fibrosis ( Fig. 5 F–H). Furthermore, fluorescent probe staining demonstrated that A1TP-HX-EVs effectively reduced levels of labile ferrous ions and ROS in the NP tissues, significantly decreasing NPC death ( Fig. S10F–H ). A1TP-HX-EVs also attenuated ferroptosis by inhibiting ferritin degradation and promoting GPX4 expression, while reducing MMP13 levels to enhance the production of the primary extracellular matrix component COL2 and limit compensatory COL1 accumulation. Moreover, ADGRG1 expression in NP tissues decreased following A1TP-HX-EVs treatment ( Fig. S10I ). Finally, A1TP-HX-EVs promoted mitochondrial regeneration and reduced the ferroptosis marker 4-HNE, indicating significant suppression of NPC ferroptosis ( Fig. 5 I–J). In summary, these results demonstrated that HX-EVs, compared with unmodified EVs, enhance NPC antioxidant capacity and reduce labile ferrous ion release. When engineered with A1TP, A1TP-HX-EVs more effectively target degenerated NPCs, further enhancing therapeutic efficacy by inhibiting ferritin degradation, promoting mitochondrial regeneration, and suppressing NPC ferroptosis. Together, these actions facilitate NP repair and help prevent the progression of IVDD.

Next, we sought to investigate the molecular mechanisms by which A1TP-HX-EVs regulate degenerative IVD repair. We performed RNA-seq to compare gene expression in primary NPCs among the control group, the TBHP-induced group, and the TBHP-induced group treated with A1TP-HX-EVs. By identifying genes downregulated following TBHP treatment and upregulated after A1TP-HX-EVs treatment, we obtained a set of 419 differentially expressed genes ( Fig. 6 A). GO enrichment analysis revealed that these differentially expressed genes are associated with mitochondrial function and anti-ferroptosis biological processes ( Fig. 6 B and S11A ). To further explore the molecular mechanisms underlying repair, KEGG enrichment analysis of genes differentially expressed between the A1TP-HX-EVs-treated and TBHP groups showed that the AMPK pathway was activated by A1TP-HX-EVs, whereas it was not enriched in the TBHP group ( Fig. 6 C and S11B ). Western blot analysis showed that A1TP-HX-EVs activated AMPK and its downstream target silent information regulator 1 (SIRT1) through phosphorylation, regulated deacetylation of downstream peroxisome proliferator activated receptor γ coactivator-1α (PGC-1α), and promoted the expression of the transcription factor Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) ( Fig. 6 D–E and S11C). Previous studies have shown that transcriptional activation of NRF2 plays a critical role in regulating ferroptosis and mitochondrial regeneration [ 32 , 33 ]. We further found that PGC-1α interacts with NRF2 to suppress the expression of NCOA4, and immunofluorescence analysis showed that, compared with EVs and HX-EVs, A1TP-HX-EVs significantly reduced ferritinophagy by downregulating NCOA4 expression, thereby limiting the release of labile ferrous ions ( Fig. 6 F). In addition, the mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), which is involved in mitochondrial repair and biogenesis, was upregulated via NRF2 activation. Electron microscopy revealed that A1TP-HX-EVs more effectively promoted the regeneration of mitochondrial cristae and maintained mitochondrial membrane integrity, reducing permeability induced by mitochondrial membrane damage ( Fig. 6 G and S11D-E ). In contrast, treatment with an AMPK inhibitor (BAY-3827) or an NRF2 inhibitor (ML385) significantly abrogated the regulatory effects of A1TP-HX-EVs on the downstream AMPK/NRF2 targets NCOA4 and TFAM ( Fig. 6 H), and failed to effectively suppress ferritinophagy and the expression of NPC injury markers ( Fig. S11F ). To further investigate the reparative effects of A1TP-HX-EVs on degenerated intervertebral discs in vivo , we established rat IVDD models and analyzed protein levels after A1TP-HX-EVs treatment. The results confirmed activation of the AMPK pathway and NRF2-mediated regulation of NCOA4 and TFAM expression ( Fig. S11G–H ). In vivo studies further demonstrated that A1TP-HX-EVs more effectively suppressed ferritinophagy, promoted structural repair of mitochondria in degenerated nucleus pulposus, reduced NPC ferroptosis, and facilitated NP regeneration following IVDD ( Fig. 6 I–J). Collectively, these findings indicated that A1TP-HX-EVs inhibit ferritinophagy and promote mitochondrial structural and functional restoration by activating the AMPK/NRF2 pathway. Recent studies have revealed that MSC-derived EVs carry a variety of bioactive small molecules capable of promoting tissue repair [ [34] , [35] , [36] ]. However, the key bioactive small molecules within HX-EVs responsible for regulating degenerative IVD repair remain unclear. Using high-resolution LC-MS/MS analysis, we compared the small-molecule composition and abundance between HX-EVs and EVs and found significant differences ( Fig. S12A–B ). In total, 106 endogenous bioactive small molecules were identified at high abundance, among which 87 were highly expressed in HX-EVs and 19 were highly enriched in EVs ( Fig. 7 A). Enrichment analysis of the highly expressed molecules in HX-EVs using the Small Molecule Pathway Database (SMPDB) revealed significant enrichment in multiple metabolic pathways related to ferroptosis inhibition and mitochondrial function ( Fig. 7 B and S12C-D ). More importantly, we found that the antioxidant molecule taurine was expressed at approximately 3.0-fold higher levels in HX-EVs than in EVs. This result was further confirmed by ELISA, and a similar difference was observed at the cellular level ( Fig. 7 C–D). Previous studies have shown that placental tissues primarily acquire taurine through active uptake from the bloodstream via the taurine transporter (TAUT), rather than through endogenous synthesis [ 37 ]. Consistent with this, we found that hypoxic treatment significantly upregulated the expression of tonicity-responsive enhancer-binding protein (TonEBP) in pMSCs. As reported, TonEBP binds to the promoter region of TAUT to enhance its transcription [ 38 ]. Our results indicate that hypoxia increases TAUT expression by regulating TonEBP ( Fig. S13A ), thereby promoting the active accumulation of taurine in pMSCs and leading to taurine enrichment in the derived HX-EVs. Engineering modification of A1TP-HX-EVs enabled more efficient delivery and increased intracellular taurine levels in NPCs by approximately 3.3-fold ( Fig. 7 E). To determine whether taurine functions as the key factor regulating AMPK/NRF2 pathway activation, we constructed a lentiviral vector to knockdown TAUT in pMSCs. This intervention significantly decreased taurine levels in HX-EVs ( Fig. 7 F–G). Notably, depletion of taurine in the targeted engineered HX-EVs (A1TP-KD-HX-EVs) markedly attenuated AMPK/NRF2 pathway activation and failed to effectively enhance TFAM expression or suppress NCOA4 expression via NRF2 ( Fig. 7 H). At the cellular level, taurine-deficient A1TP-KD-HX-EVs failed to effectively reverse mitochondrial permeability or reduce ferrous ion release, leading to impaired mitochondrial regeneration. Consequently, they were unable to decrease intracellular ROS and lipid peroxidation levels, resulting in ineffective suppression of TBHP-induced ferroptosis in NPCs ( Fig. 7 I and S13B-D ). Interestingly, by overexpressing the key rate-limiting enzyme CDO1 involved in taurine synthesis in pMSCs using a lentiviral system, the taurine content in the derived EVs was markedly increased ( Fig. 7 J–K). After A1TP engineering, these taurine-enriched EVs (A1TP-OE-EVs) effectively reversed the relatively weak reparative effects of EVs ( Fig. 7 L–M), significantly suppressing ferrous ion release and ROS-induced ferroptosis in NPCs ( Fig. S13E–G ). Finally, mitochondrial stress testing further confirmed that the engineered A1TP-HX-EVs primarily mediate mitochondrial functional repair through their taurine enrichment. Moreover, increasing taurine loading in EVs and delivering them via A1TP targeting achieved a comparable reparative effect to that of A1TP-HX-EVs ( Fig. 7 N–O), indicating that taurine plays a dominant role in the HX-EV-mediated repair process.

In fact, we also investigated whether direct administration of the A1TP peptide or taurine alone could achieve comparable therapeutic effects. In vitro results showed that, unlike A1TP-HX-EVs, A1TP alone failed to activate the AMPK/NRF2 signaling pathway to promote mitochondrial regeneration or suppress ROS-induced ferroptosis in NPCs. Similarly, treatment with an equivalent concentration of taurine resulted in markedly weaker therapeutic effects ( Fig. S14A–B ), exhibiting substantially reduced mitochondrial repair compared with A1TP-HX-EVs ( Fig. S14C–F ). To explore why direct taurine administration was low effective, we found that NPCs express minimal levels of the TAUT ( Fig. S14G–H ), thereby limiting taurine uptake efficiency ( Fig. S14I ) and diminishing its reparative potential. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that A1TP-HX-EVs mediate targeted delivery of taurine, which activates the AMPK/NRF2 pathway to suppress ferroptosis and promote mitochondrial regeneration in NPCs, thereby facilitating the repair of ROS-injured cells.

Next, we sought to elucidate the molecular mechanism by which taurine regulates the activation of the AMPK/NRF2 signaling pathway to promote the repair of degenerated NP tissue. Previous studies have shown that the activation of the AMPK pathway is primarily regulated by the binding of Ca 2+ to CaMKKβ and the formation of the LKB1(Liver Kinase B1)-STRAD(STE-20-related Kinase Adaptor Protein)-MO25(Mouse Protein 25) kinase complex [ 39 ]. Our results indicated that taurine did not alter Ca 2+ influx ( Fig. S15A ), suggesting that Ca 2+ and its binding to CaMKKβ are unlikely to be the primary mechanisms underlying taurine-induced activation of the AMPK/NRF2 pathway. Interestingly, structural studies revealed that sulfate ions bind within the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex at specific sites on LKB1 (Lys108) and MO25 (Arg194 and Arg152) [ 40 ]. Molecular dynamics simulations further indicated that sulfate ions enhance the stability of the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex by increasing hydrogen bond formation between LKB1 and STRAD-MO25 ( Fig. S15B–C ). Given that taurine contains a terminal sulfonic acid group resembling a sulfate moiety, we hypothesized that taurine may promote the formation of the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex through this structural feature. Subsequently, immunoprecipitation followed by LC-MS/MS analysis revealed strong interactions between taurine and both LKB1 and MO25 ( Fig. 8 A). Biochemically, in vitro binding assays demonstrated a direct interaction between purified LKB1 and MO25 protein and Taurine, in contrast, LKB1 and MO25 mutants abrogated the capacity of binding with Taurine ( Fig. 8 B–C and S 15D). To elucidate the binding mechanism, we performed induced-fit docking (IFD) simulations between taurine and the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex. Twenty potential binding conformations were identified and ranked based on the Induced Fit Docking score (IFD Score) and binding affinity (XP GScore), from which five models were selected as the most plausible binding modes ( Fig. S15E–F ). Metadynamics simulations further indicated that the IFD2 conformation exhibited the highest binding stability ( Fig. 8 D), while molecular dynamics analysis confirmed that IFD2 had the most favorable binding free energy ( Fig. 8 D and S15G ). In the proposed model, the sulfonic acid group of taurine forms hydrogen bonds with LKB1 (Arg301) and MO25 (Leu197) sites, its amino group forms hydrogen bonds with LKB1 (Glu165) and MO25 (Arg194) sites, and a salt bridge with LKB1 (Glu165) site ( Fig. 8 E). Notably, these mutations significantly reduced taurine binding to both LKB1 and MO25 ( Fig. 8 F) and markedly decreased the interaction between LKB1 and MO25, thereby impairing the formation of the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex ( Fig. 8 G). Since the activation of AMPK primarily depends on the formation of the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex, which regulates the kinase activity of LKB1. The reduction in the binding between LKB1 and MO25 weakens LKB1 kinase activation [ 40 , 41 ]. Mutation of the taurine-binding sites in LKB1 and MO25 markedly attenuated the ability of A1TP-HX-EVs to inhibit ferritinophagy and ferrous ion release, and abolished their effect on restoring GPX4 expression ( Fig. 8 H and S16B-C ). Moreover, these mutations significantly impaired the activation of the AMPK/NRF2 pathway by A1TP-HX-EVs ( Fig. 8 I), weakened TFAM-mediated mitochondrial structural and functional repair ( Fig. 8 J–L), and failed to effectively suppress ROS accumulation and lipid peroxidation-induced ferroptosis in NPCs ( Fig. S16D–E ). In summary, our findings demonstrated that A1TP-HX-EVs deliver high levels of the multifunctional amino acid derivative taurine, which binds to the LKB1 (Glu165, Arg301) and MO25 (Arg194, Leu197) residues. This interaction promotes the formation of the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 kinase complex, activates LKB1 kinase activity, and subsequently triggers the downstream AMPK/NRF2 signaling pathway. Through this mechanism, A1TP-HX-EVs inhibit ferritinophagy and promote mitochondrial regeneration, which reduces ROS-induced ferroptosis in NPCs.
sections.discussion:
Elucidating the crucial pathophysiological mechanisms underlying nucleus pulposus cell injury is critical for developing effective therapeutic strategies for IVDD and minimizing subsequent spinal cascade damage. Oxidative stress is closely linked to IVD inflammation, cellular senescence, autophagy, and epigenetic regulation of IVD cells. These pathological processes converge on a common mediator, ROS, which interacts synergistically during IVDD to drive disease progression [ 6 ]. In the IVDD process, factors such as cellular senescence, mechanical stress, and inflammatory responses can trigger early increases in ROS levels within NPCs [ 8 , 9 ]. Elevated ROS further damages mitochondrial DNA and proteins, causing mitochondrial dysfunction and establishing a vicious cycle of ROS production [ 42 ]. Moreover, ROS oxidatively modifies amino acid residues in ferritin and disrupts its structure, promoting ferritin degradation and the release of labile ferrous ions, which drives hydroxyl radical generation via the Fenton reaction, thereby inducing ferroptosis [ 43 ]. Excess ferrous ions, in turn, provide positive feedback to enhance ROS generation, exacerbating oxidative damage and mitochondrial abnormalities [ 44 ]. Our findings demonstrate that an oxidative stress damage driven by "ROS-Mitochondrial dysfunction-Ferritinophagy" feedback loop acts as a central driver, accelerating NPC ferroptosis and ECM degradation, which promotes promoting IVDD progression. Targeted interventions aimed at this loop show potential for reversing IVDD.

In this study, we identified the aGPCR family protein ADGRG1 as an early-warning molecule indicating initial IVDD. Although knockdown of ADGRG1 did not directly suppress oxidative stress feedback loop-driven NPC injury, nor did it significantly increase susceptibility to ROS-induced ferroptosis, emerging evidence suggests a regulatory role for ADGRG1 in redox homeostasis. Studies in enriched functional human hematopoietic stem cells have reported a negative correlation between ADGRG1 expression and mitochondrial ROS levels [ 16 ]. Moreover, activation of ADGRG1 has been shown to attenuate lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis in hepatocytes induced by doxorubicin or ischemia–reperfusion injury [ 45 ]. Therefore, we speculate that upregulation of ADGRG1 in NPCs may contribute to cellular resistance against oxidative stress. Our study demonstrated that the ADGRG1-tethered peptide (A1TP) alone is insufficient to effectively activate ADGRG1 to suppress oxidative stress feedback loop–mediated ferroptosis. However, A1TP enables specific targeting and binding to ADGRG1. Accordingly, we characterize ADGRG1 as an oxidative stress–induced ferroptosis marker following NPC injury and exploit it as a recognition target for targeted delivery strategies. We modified antioxidant HX-EVs with an A1TP to specifically target and anchor injured NPCs, which promotes EV internalization. Our results demonstrated that A1TP-HX-EVs attenuate NPC damage by reducing ferritinophagy and promoting mitochondrial repair, thereby interrupting the oxidative stress feedback loop, improving NP-ECM composition, inhibiting maladaptive repair and fibrosis, and ultimately providing significant intervertebral disc protection. Moreover, owing to advances in solid-phase peptide synthesis, the A1TP peptide offers several practical advantages, including facile synthesis, low production cost, high-throughput scalability, and ease of functional customization [ 46 ]. Compared with ADGRG1 antibodies, A1TP peptides are therefore more suitable for engineering EV-based targeted delivery systems. By loading Gaussia luciferase into A1TP-HX-EVs, we were able to quantify the amount of uninternalized EVs in degenerative discs, enabling assessment of IVDD severity and prediction of long-term therapeutic efficacy-highlighting the potential clinical translational value of this strategy.

Extracellular vesicles derived from stem cells mediate intercellular communication by transferring bioactive molecules and have demonstrated remarkable therapeutic potential in tissue repair following injury [ 47 ]. Recent studies have revealed that, in addition to macromolecules such as DNA, RNA and proteins, MSC-derived EVs carry a range of bioactive small molecules, including fatty acids, choline, amino acid derivatives, and various metabolites, play crucial roles in tissue repair [ [34] , [35] , [36] ], However, the specific bioactive small molecules involved in regulating IVDD repair remain unclear. Our study found that hypoxic preconditioning upregulated the expression of TonEBP in pMSCs, which in turn enhanced TAUT expression and taurine uptake, leading to increased taurine enrichment in HX-EVs. Taurine is known to play vital roles in osmoregulation, cytoprotection, and attenuation of oxidative stress [ 48 ]. In models of renal and cardiac injury, taurine has been proven to suppress ROS-dependent autophagy and cellular damage by modulating the Akt/mTOR and MAPK signaling pathways [ 49 , 50 ]. Interestingly, our results revealed that A1TP-HX-EVs delivering high levels of taurine activated the AMPK signaling pathway, promoting PGC-1α deacetylation and regulating NRF2 expression. Previous studies have demonstrated that NRF2 could upregulate the E3 ubiquitin ligase HERC2, which mediates the ubiquitination and degradation of NCOA4, a key regulator of ferritinophagy [ 24 , 32 ]. Moreover, PGC-1α cooperates with NRF2 to transcriptionally co-activate TFAM expression [ 33 ]. Our findings confirmed that targeted delivery of taurine activates the AMPK/NRF2 signaling axis, which reduces NCOA4-mediated ferritinophagy and enhances mitochondrial repair and biogenesis through NRF2-dependent TFAM upregulation. Collectively, targeted taurine delivery suppresses the oxidative stress feedback loop and promotes NP tissue regeneration following IVDD through dual regulatory mechanisms.

Notably, taurine does not directly scavenge ROS, instead, it reduces ROS levels and cellular damage by modulating oxidative stress responses and enhancing antioxidant defenses [ 49 , 51 ]. Jia et al. demonstrated in cortical neuron repair that taurine promotes the expression of PGC-1α and TFAM, which stimulates mitochondrial DNA synthesis and the formation of new mitochondria [ 52 ]. However, the precise molecular regulatory mechanisms underlying these effects remain unclear. Previous studies have shown that downstream signaling of AMPK/NRF2 activation primarily involves phosphorylation, acetylation, and transcription factor-mediated regulation of target gene expression, while its upstream activation is mainly governed by Ca 2+ /CaMKKβ interactions and the assembly of the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 kinase complex [ 39 ]. We found that the taurine delivered by A1TP-HX-EVs did not activate AMPK through regulation of intracellular Ca 2+ levels in NPCs. Interestingly, Zeqiraj et al. reported that sulfate ions within the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex form hydrogen and salt bonds with residues in LKB1 and MO25 [ 40 ]. MO25 acts as a scaffolding protein that stabilizes the interaction between LKB1 and STRAD, enhances LKB1's kinase activity, and is involved in the complex's structural integrity [ 39 , 40 ]. Structural analysis revealed that the presence of sulfate ions promotes a more stable conformation of the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 kinase complex. Given the structural similarity between taurine and sulfate ions, further investigation demonstrated that taurine can form hydrogen and salt bonds with LKB1 (Glu165, Arg301) and MO25 (Arg194, Leu197) residues, facilitating the assembly of the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex. This interaction enhances LKB1 kinase activity and subsequently activates the AMPK/NRF2 signaling pathway, which disrupts the oxidative stress-induced positive feedback loop in NPCs. Our findings reveal a novel regulatory mechanism by which taurine, delivered via hypoxia-induced stem cell-derived EVs, activates the AMPK/NRF2 pathway and provides new insight into how taurine suppresses ferritinophagy and promotes mitochondrial regeneration.

In addition, intervertebral disc degeneration is a systemic and highly regulated process that involves complex molecular and cellular interactions and signaling networks [ 53 , 54 ]. Although we provide evidence linking taurine within HX-EVs to nucleus pulposus repair and regeneration, other regulatory cargos carried by HX-EVs, such as nucleic acids (e.g., DNA and microRNAs), cytokines (including IL-10 and IGF-1), enzymes, or additional metabolites, may also act synergistically or independently to mediate mitochondrial regeneration, extracellular matrix remodeling, and inflammatory modulation [ 55 ]. Such multifactorial contributions are likely to be particularly important in the complex ROS-driven microenvironment associated with mechanical injury and age-related degeneration. Furthermore, recent studies have identified 17α-hydroxypregnenolone as an agonist of ADGRG1 that antagonizes ferroptosis and effectively attenuates liver injury when administered either before or after injury [ 45 ]. Although binding of the A1TP peptide monomer to ADGRG1 did not directly regulate ferroptosis or mitochondrial repair in our study, it remains unclear whether A1TP influences cellular repair processes through activation of ADGRG1 via alternative mechanisms. Future studies are needed to determine whether G protein-coupled receptor–associated signaling pathways participate in HX-EV-mediated intervertebral disc repair. Moreover, ADGRG1 is expressed in multiple tissues and cell types, including immune cells and neurons, etc [ 56 ]. Although A1TP-modified HX-EVs in this study were administered via local intradiscal injection and short-term results indicated limited distribution to extra-discal organs, suggesting a low risk of off-target effects, severe disc degeneration is often accompanied by neovascularization, raising the possibility of diffusion and systemic accumulation. Long-term studies are required to evaluate the feasibility and safety of repeated intradiscal administration.
sections.conclusion: In summary, the oxidative stress feedback loop formed among ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction, and ferroptosis plays a critical role in nucleus pulposus injury, continuously accelerating the progression of IVDD. We first revealed the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor ADGRG1, which is highly expressed on the membrane of degenerative nucleus pulposus cells, as a promising diagnostic and therapeutic target for ROS-induced IVDD. In this study, we engineered ADGRG1-tethered peptide-modified hypoxia-induced pMSC-derived extracellular vesicles (A1TP-HX-EVs) to enhance the targeted delivery efficiency of therapeutic EVs to degenerated discs. A1TP-HX-EVs specifically delivered hypoxia-enriched taurine to injured NPCs, promoting the assembly of the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 kinase complex and activating the AMPK/NRF2 signaling pathway. This activation suppressed ferritinophagy, enhanced mitochondrial repair and regeneration, and ultimately reversed the ROS-induced ferroptosis and extracellular matrix-degrading microenvironment, restoring IVD structure and function. This model paves the way for IVD protection and the therapeutic potential of HX-EVs through targeted disruption of the oxidative stress feedback cycle in nucleus pulposus cells.
